title: Value Forcing: Aligning Return Distributions at All Noise Levels

paper.title: Value Forcing: Aligning Return Distributions at All Noise Levels
paper.abstract:
Abstract Learning accurate value functions is central to reinforcement learning (RL), yet remains challenging because supervision is limited and indirect: ground-truth values are unavailable, and each transition in the data only provides an immediate reward that can be used to construct bootstrapped targets as supervision. This challenge is particularly pronounced when data is limited or reward signals are sparse, as is common in real-world applications such as robotics.
We argue that the key to accurate value learning in this limited data regime is extracting richer learning signals from the available data. In this paper, we introduce Value Forcing , a new approach that uses flow matching to estimate return distributions and enables accurate value learning from limited data. Our key insight is that we can extract richer learning signals by enforcing Bellman consistency at every noise level. Empirically, Value Forcing improves the accuracy of estimating the return distribution, and prevents the distribution from collapsing to a single value, as occurs with prior methods. We instantiate Value Forcing with two practical value-learning algorithms: VF, an actor-critic method, and IVF, an implicit value-learning method. We evaluate both algorithms across 26 26 long-horizon tasks in the offline RL setting and find that they outperform prior value-learning methods, with particularly large gains when data is limited. Our project website is available at https://chongyi-zheng.github.io/value-forcing .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: We introduce Value Forcing , a new approach to learning distributional value functions with flow matching that supervises the learned return distribution at every flow noise level through Bellman consistency. Unlike prior methods that provide supervision only at selected noise levels or use inaccurate targets at others, Value Forcing provides substantially richer learning signals and enables much more accurate estimation of the return distribution, preventing it from collapsing around a single value. This in turn leads to better policy performance, especially in the limited-data regime. Value estimation lies at the heart of reinforcement learning (RL): value functions estimate the expected return of following a certain course of actions, guiding agents to select better actions that improve long-term returns. However, accurately estimating the values is hard, especially with limited amounts of data or if the reward feedback is sparse. Supervision for long-term value is limited and indirect: each observed transition provides only an immediate reward, but no ground-truth expected return. Temporal-difference (TD) methods construct prediction targets using their own value estimates, which could be inaccurate and bias learning. With limited data, there is little room to correct these errors. However, such settings are common in real-world applications such as robotics. This raises the question: is there a way to extract richer learning signals from limited available transitions? Many widely used RL methods ( Mnih et al., 2015 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) learn scalar value functions that summarize the future outcome of a policy. This scheme has limited expressivity and may give a sparse supervision signal when used as the target for TD learning. Distributional RL instead models the full return distribution and can provide richer learning signals when the whole return distribution is used as the TD target ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Rowland et al., 2023 ) . For example, an action that produces returns of − 1 -1 and + 1 +1 with equal probability has the same expected return as another action that always produces 0 0 return, yet their distributions differ. Learning to distinguish these two actions and their outcomes can enable more effective use of the available data. Recent work has begun to use modern generative models such as flow matching to represent the return distribution. These methods learn to map Gaussian noise to the return distribution through an iterative denoising process. Beyond capturing complex return distributions, flow matching also creates an opportunity to provide even richer supervision by learning at different noise levels ( Farebrother et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . However, prior flow-based return estimators typically only provide supervision using the endpoint of the flow path ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2025 ; Groom et al., 2026 ; Agrawalla et al., 2026 ) , missing the opportunity to supervise all other noise levels. While others have explored applying Bellman consistency at all noise levels, they either suffer from enforcing an incorrect consistency at the initial flow step ( Dong et al., 2025 ) or only apply the consistency along the flow paths starting from the same noise ( Xu et al., 2026 ) (Fig. 1 (Center) ). Empirically, we find that sparse supervision or incorrect dense supervision can lead to inaccurate modeling of the return distribution, and often results in the learned return distribution collapsing toward a point mass (see Fig. 2 ), thereby undermining the effectiveness of distributional value learning. In this paper, we introduce Value Forcing, a new distributional value learning approach that enforces Bellman consistency at every noise level (see illustration in Fig. 1 ). At each noise level, Value Forcing uses the next-state marginal return distribution to supervise the current-state marginal return distribution. Unlike the standard Bellman operator, we introduce a new flow Bellman operator that includes a Gaussian correction. We show that Value Forcing has a unique fixed point at every noise level, preserving the initial Gaussian noise and recovering the distributional Bellman equation in the denoised space. Empirically, we find that Value Forcing can model the return distribution much more accurately compared to the prior methods and does not suffer from distribution collapse (Fig. 1 ). We instantiate two practical value-learning algorithms with Value Forcing: VF, an actor-critic algorithm, and IVF, an implicit method via expectile-weighted flow matching. Theoretically, we show that IVF approaches the optimal value within actions presented in the dataset as the expectile increases. Empirically, we evaluate both VF and IVF across 26 26 long-horizon tasks, 20 20 from OGBench and 6 6 from OCBench, and show that they improve return estimation and policy performance over prior flow-based value learning methods, with particularly strong gains when data is limited.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Offline RL aims to learn a reward-maximizing policy from a fixed offline dataset. The core challenge in this setting is to learn a value function while preventing erroneous extrapolation outside the distribution of the dataset. Previous works have proposed strategies based on applying conservative penalties for out-of-distribution samples ( Kumar et al., 2020 ; Nakamoto et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2022 ; Chae et al., 2026 ) , constraining action selection in Bellman backups to the dataset support ( Fujimoto et al., 2019 ; Kumar et al., 2019 ; Singh et al., 2022 ) , or not querying samples outside the offline dataset at all ( Kostrikov et al., 2022 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . While most previous works focus on training an accurate value function with the entire offline dataset, we focus on the setting with extremely limited offline data. Most similar to our focus is the work of Xu et al. (2023) ; Park et al. (2026) , which also compares different value learning algorithms on subsets of the entire offline datasets. However, these methods learn a scalar return value, while we aim to learn the whole distribution of the return value using flow matching. This offers denser supervision during TD updates, and in practice leads to better performance in the limited dataset setting. We find that our method matches the state of the art on the full dataset, but outperforms it by a large margin when data is more limited. Distributional and generative value functions. Distributional value functions aim to learn the entire distribution of the discounted cumulative return instead of a single scalar that estimates its expected value ( Bellemare et al., 2017 ; Bellemare et al., 2023 ) . Early methods model the value distribution as a discrete categorical distribution ( Bellemare et al., 2017 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Dabney et al., 2018b ) or continuous distributions with restrictive modeling assumptions ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Dabney et al., 2018a ) . Recent methods have leveraged diffusion and flow matching to represent complex return distributions ( Dong et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Espinosa-Dice et al., 2025 ) and their expected values ( Agrawalla et al., 2026 ) . Our method falls into the former category, where methods differ primarily in where the Bellman consistency is enforced in the denoising path. DFC ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , FlowCritic ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) , FlowIQN ( Groom et al., 2026 ) , and Dual-Flow RL ( Li et al., 2026 ) enforce the Bellman consistency at the endpoint of the flow, where the Bellman target is computed in the denoised space and used as a flow-matching target for all noise levels. FlowIQN further introduces a quantile-aligned coupling between initial noises and final samples. Dong et al. (2025) , Espinosa-Dice et al. (2025) , and Xu et al. (2026) introduce stronger constraints along the flow path: Value Flows ( Dong et al., 2025 ) and EVOR ( Espinosa-Dice et al., 2025 ) use the velocity field directly as the TD bootstrapping target, but naïvely apply the clean Bellman equation at all noise levels; PCBF ( Xu et al., 2026 ) couples two flow paths using the same initial noise and applies the Bellman operator at all noise levels along the coupled paths, but the marginal flow paths lack Bellman consistency because of the coupling. In contrast, our method enforces the Bellman consistency at all noise levels. We achieve this by defining a flow Bellman operator whose fixed point aligns the return distributions at every noise level. We find that this results in much more accurate return estimation, especially in the low-data regime. See the Appendix Table 1 for a summary of these differences.

sections.heading: 4 Bellman consistency at all noise levels
sections.text: Our goal is to extract richer learning signals from each transition in the data. To achieve this goal, we incorporate Bellman consistency throughout the return flow paths by introducing a novel flow Bellman operator that depends on the noise level (Sec. 4.1 ). We first derive this operator below, and show that it is consistent with the standard Bellman operator at the flow endpoints and has a unique fixed point at all noise levels. We then use this flow Bellman operator to derive practical flow-matching losses in Sec. 4.2 .

sections.heading: 5 Value Forcing algorithms

We consider two ways to turn the richer distributional learning signals of Value Forcing into RL algorithms. We refer to this approach as the explicit method, and introduce a practical algorithm named VF. sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: We conduct experiments to study how well Value Forcing can learn the return distribution on a range of challenging long-horizon tasks. Concretely, we ask the research questions: (1) Does Value Forcing improve return estimation accuracy? (2) How do VF and IVF compare to prior offline RL methods across different dataset sizes? (3) What are the important design decisions in VF and IVF? Experimental setup. We evaluate our methods on 20 20 tasks from OGBench ( Park et al., 2024 ) and 6 6 tasks from OCBench ( Park & Levine, 2026 ) in the offline RL setting. OGBench includes 4 4 domains with 5 5 tasks each: cube-triple , cube-quadruple , puzzle-4x4 , and humanoidmaze-giant . OCBench includes 1 1 task from block-lite-single , 2 2 from block-lite-double , and 3 3 from chamber-lite-easy . We adopt action chunking ( Li et al., 2025 ) , where the policy predicts and executes a sequence of actions before predicting the next sequence. The resulting higher-dimensional action space makes value learning more challenging. Following Zhou et al. (2026) , we use the OGBench datasets with 100 100 M transitions as the full offline datasets and experiment with subsets of them, ranging from 10 % 10\% to 100 % 100\% , to study the effectiveness of different value learning methods on decreasing dataset sizes. For OCBench, we compare our methods with selected baselines using 25 % 25\% and 100 % 100\% of the available data. We report the mean and standard deviation across 4 4 random seeds for all experiments. See Appendix D.1 for details on dataset construction and evaluation protocols. Comparisons. We compare VF and IVF with prior value learning methods, grouped into explicit or implicit methods. For explicit methods, we compare VF against prior methods that explicitly learn a policy using flow-based distributional critics FlowCritic ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) , Value Flows ( Dong et al., 2025 ) , PCBF ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , categorical distributional critic C51 ( Bellemare et al., 2017 ) , quantile distributional critic IQN ( Dabney et al., 2018a ) , flow-based non-distributional critic Floq ( Agrawalla et al., 2026 ) , and scalar critic QC . For implicit methods , we compare IVF against prior methods that perform implicit value learning. Since there are no prior implicit flow-based distributional methods, we compare against categorical distributional critics DIVL ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , our novel adaptations of C51 and IQN termed Implicit C51 and Implicit IQN , and scalar critic Implicit QC . For OCBench experiments, we compare VF with representative baselines Value Flows, C51, and QC, and compare IVF with Implicit C51 and Implicit QC. See Appendix D.2 for details of each prior method.

sections.heading: 6.1 Value Forcing improves return estimation accuracy
sections.text: Figure 2: Value Forcing learns more accurate return distributions than prior flow-based return estimators. (Left) We collect datasets to conduct policy evaluation experiments at a single state from each of the four OGBench domains. (Center) Value Forcing captures the ground-truth return distributions more accurately, while prior methods are biased and collapse their predictions into narrow peaks. (Right) Value Forcing achieves lower mean 1 1 -Wasserstein distances than all three prior methods in all tasks. We investigate whether Value Forcing improves return distribution prediction by conducting policy evaluation experiments comparing VF with Value Flows, FlowCritic, and PCBF at a single state randomly sampled from each of the four OGBench domains. Our goal is to compare the return estimation accuracy starting from a single state in each domain and then following a fixed policy. Specifically, from each state, we execute a fixed starting action chunk and then roll out a data-collection policy to collect 1000 1000 training trajectories and 1000 1000 evaluation trajectories separately. We train each method on the training trajectories, using the recorded actions in the bootstrap targets, effectively performing SARSA ( Sutton et al., 1998 ) . For evaluation, we use discounted returns from the evaluation trajectories as the ground truth. Thus, all methods evaluate the same data-collection policy. Following Dong et al. (2025) , we visualize the predicted return distributions and measure their 1 1 -Wasserstein distances to the ground-truth returns. As a reference, an Oracle return estimator fits the realized returns of the same trajectories using the standard flow-matching loss (Eq. 3 ). This provides a reference for errors other than bootstrapping: function approximation, optimization, finite samples, etc. See Appendix D.4 for the full experimental details. Fig. 2 shows that VF achieves lower mean 1 1 -Wasserstein distances than previous flow-based critics on all four tasks. Observe that VF captures more of the ground-truth spread, while Value Flows and FlowCritic concentrate their predictions into narrow peaks. PCBF produces broader predictions on the cube tasks, but still misses much of the ground-truth spread. Relative to PCBF, VF reduces the mean 1 1 -Wasserstein distance by 81 % 81\% on puzzle-4x4 and 89 % 89\% on humanoidmaze-giant . On cube-triple and puzzle-4x4 , VF’s 1 1 -Wasserstein distances are also close to the Oracle . In particular, VF corrects Value Flows’ inconsistent supervision at τ = 0 \tau=0 , offering an explanation for the improvement over its narrow, shifted predictions. In Appendix Fig. 7 , we visualize the return flow paths at different noise levels, showing that VF spreads its return paths at early noise levels (around τ = 0.25 \tau=0.25 ), while baselines collapse (around τ = 0.9 \tau=0.9 ). The gains over FlowCritic and PCBF further suggest the benefit of enforcing Bellman consistency of noisy return distributions at every noise level.

sections.heading: 6.2 VF and IVF outperform prior offline RL methods on smaller datasets
sections.text: We next compare VF and IVF against prior value-learning algorithms under varying dataset sizes to evaluate different methods as data get increasingly limited. On OGBench, we train each method using the full dataset as well as subsets containing 50 % 50\% , 25 % 25\% , and 10 % 10\% of the available transitions. We construct these subsets by sampling trajectories using a softmax over their average rewards (Appendix D.1 ). We additionally evaluate the methods on OCBench using 25 % 25\% and 100 % 100\% of the available data. Fig. 3 summarizes the success rates on both benchmarks, grouping the methods into explicit and implicit methods. On OGBench, VF achieves the highest mean success rates with 10 % 10\% and 25 % 25\% of the data and performs similarly to the strongest baseline methods at larger dataset sizes. Most prior flow-based distributional RL methods significantly underperform VF, and even the scalar critic QC. This difference is especially prominent with 10 % 10\% of the data, highlighting the importance of Bellman consistency at all noise levels; not doing so makes the flow-based distributional baselines perform even worse than the scalar critic. In contrast, VF barely performs worse as the dataset size decreases. Among implicit methods, IVF performs comparably to the strongest baselines on the full dataset and achieves higher mean success rates than all prior methods at every reduced dataset size. On OCBench, VF achieves the highest mean success rates among the evaluated explicit methods with both 25 % 25\% and 100 % 100\% of the data, while IVF leads among implicit methods on the full dataset and performs comparably to the baselines with 25 % 25\% of the data. These results suggest that aligning return distributions at all noise levels is incredibly important for training flow-based distributional critics, and is especially beneficial when offline data is limited. Figure 3: Value Forcing improves offline RL performance across dataset sizes. Success rates are averaged over 20 20 OGBench tasks (Left) and 6 6 OCBench tasks (Right) at each dataset size. On OGBench, VF and IVF outperform their explicit and implicit baselines at 10 % 10\% and 25 % 25\% of the data, and remain competitive with more data. On OCBench, VF outperforms selected explicit methods on 25 % 25\% of the dataset, while IVF leads among selected implicit methods on the full dataset. Hatched bars ( ) indicate distributional RL methods without flow matching. See Appendix C for complete results.

sections.heading: 6.3 Key design decisions in Value Forcing
sections.text: Figure 4: Comparisons of alternative Value Forcing instantiations for explicit methods (Left) and implicit methods (Right). Figure 5: Reward scaling improves VF and IVF. Both VF and IVF achieve substantially higher success rates with reward scaling ( w/ ) than without it ( w/o ). Finally, we study key design decisions for VF and IVF by ablating them on tasks 2 2 and 4 4 from cube-triple and puzzle-4x4 . These ablations highlight the importance of policy extraction, expectile weighting, and reward scaling, while showing flexibility in the choice of bootstrap update for VF. Appendix D.5 provides experimental details and descriptions of each ablation. For VF, we ablate two alternative designs: removing the separate V V -velocity in Eq. 13 and instead using Q Q -velocity to bootstrap itself ( v Q v_{Q} only ), and replacing rejection sampling with a learned one-step actor that maximizes the Q estimate ( Park et al., 2025b ) ( one-step actor ). Fig. 5 (Left) shows that only learning v Q v_{Q} yields similar success rates to VF, whereas using a one-step actor reduces success rates by 44 % 44\% . These results suggest that VF learning a separate V-velocity is optional, while the choice of policy extraction has a larger effect on VF. For IVF, we examine alternatives to the expectile weighting in the V V -velocity loss (Eq. 16 ). We compare weighting based on scalar advantages ( Q , V Q,V expectile ) against applying expectile regression directly to velocity residuals ( v Q , v V v_{Q},v_{V} expectile ) or weighting based on return quantiles ( quantile weight ). Fig. 5 (Right) shows that weighting based on scalar advantages achieves much higher success rates than its two counterparts. These results support using scalar advantages to determine the expectile weights when learning return velocities. Finally, Fig. 5 examines the effect of reward scaling in Eq. 13 . Removing scaling reduces mean success rates from approximately 86 % 86\% to 11 % 11\% for VF and from 76 % 76\% to 11 % 11\% for IVF, highlighting the importance of reward scaling in the practical implementation of both methods.

sections.heading: Additional experiments.
sections.text: In Appendix B.2 , we examine the effects of the number of flow integration steps and return samples used to estimate V V and Q Q , showing that both VF and IVF maintain similar performance across the tested settings. We also extend the return estimation experiments in Sec. 6.1 to implicit distributional RL baselines. Appendix Fig. 6 shows that IVF better captures the ground-truth return distributions and achieves lower mean 1 1 -Wasserstein distances than alternative implicit methods.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we propose Value Forcing, a new approach to learning distributional value functions with flow matching that enforces Bellman consistency at every noise level. This provides richer supervision during training, enabling more accurate estimation of return distributions and better policy performance, especially in the limited-data regime. Our results suggest two directions for future work. First, our theoretical analysis of IVF assumes exact optimization and convergence to a self-consistent fixed point. Establishing convergence guarantees for practical algorithms with neural network approximation is an open problem. Second, extending Value Forcing to online learning and real-world applications, such as robotics, is another promising direction for future work.

sections.heading: A.2 Theoretical analyses of IVF
sections.text: We conduct theoretical analyses to examine the behavior of the expectile-weighted regression objective in Eq. 16 . Our analyses answer two questions: Q1. Does the V V -velocity that minimizes the expectile-weighted loss induce a V V -estimate that is the expectile of the Q Q -estimate? Q2. Does increasing the expectile recover the optimal value within the support of the dataset? We proceed by first discussing the setup of optimization and assumptions about the fixed point of the expectile-weighted regression objective. We then show that minimizing the expectile-weighted loss ℒ μ {\mathcal{L}}^{\mu} fits the return velocities of an implicit policy ( Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Sikchi et al., 2024 ) . Moreover, at the fixed point, the V V -estimate and the Q Q -estimate induced by the return velocities satisfy the expectile Bellman equations as in Kostrikov et al. (2022) . Finally, we show that as the expectile μ \mu approaches 1 1 , the induced V V -estimate converges to the optimal value function within the support of the dataset, as in Theorem 3 of Kostrikov et al. (2022) .

sections.heading: Optimization setup.
sections.text: We consider an optimization procedure similar to Fitted Q iteration ( Ernst et al., 2005 ) : at each iteration k k , we learn the V V -velocity v V k v^{k}_{V} and the Q Q -velocity v Q k v_{Q}^{k} using the V V -velocity v V k − 1 v_{V}^{k-1} and the Q Q -velocity v Q k − 1 v_{Q}^{k-1} from the previous iteration. Here, k = 1 , 2 , ⋯ k=1,2,\cdots indexes the iterations, with k = 0 k=0 denoting random initialization. We consider learning v V k v^{k}_{V} until convergence and then increase the number of iterations. In practice, we perform one gradient update at each iteration, which preserves a similar global convergence guarantee ( Gaur et al., 2023 ; Cai et al., 2020 ) . sections.heading: B.1 Visualizing return flows across noise levels
sections.text: Figure 7: Value Forcing learns return flows that better capture the spread of ground-truth returns. Following the policy evaluation experiments in Sec. 6.1 , we compare the return flow paths of VF ( Col 1 ), FlowCritic ( Col 2 ), Value Flows ( Col 3 ), and PCBF ( Col 4 ) from Gaussian noise ( τ = 0 \tau=0 ) to predicted returns ( τ = 1 \tau=1 ). VF spreads its return paths at early noise levels (around τ = 0.25 \tau=0.25 ), while baselines concentrate their return paths close to the flow endpoint (around τ = 0.9 \tau=0.9 ). We next examine how the learned flows transport Gaussian noise into return predictions. Following the policy evaluation setup in Sec. 6.1 , we compare VF, FlowCritic, Value Flows, and PCBF at the same state from each domain, with a fixed starting action chunk. For each method, we sample initial noise z 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) z^{0}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1) and numerically integrate the learned Q Q -velocities from τ = 0 \tau=0 to τ = 1 \tau=1 with 10 10 Euler steps, recording the intermediate noisy return z τ z^{\tau} . We draw the return flow paths of 51 51 return samples starting from the 0 0 th, 2 2 nd, 4 4 th, …, 100 100 th quantiles of the Gaussian distribution. We also plot the initial noise density and the predicted return density, together with the ground-truth return density at the endpoint. We show return predictions that span from the 5 5 th percentile of the ground-truth returns to the largest return, extended to cover every Value Flows prediction. Fig. 7 shows the evolutions of return flow paths. Although all methods start from Gaussian noise, VF preserves flow paths that lead to different regions of the return distribution. FlowCritic and Value Flows instead concentrate many flow paths toward a common return value as the noise level approaches 1 1 . PCBF produces broader predictions on the cube domains, but its endpoint distributions remain overly concentrated, particularly on puzzle-4x4 and humanoidmaze-giant . In addition, different methods also differ in where their trajectories terminate. On cube-quadruple and humanoidmaze-giant , FlowCritic underestimates the return distribution, while Value Flows overestimates it. PCBF places its predictions closer to the ground-truth peak on humanoidmaze-giant , but still misses much of the return spread. VF captures both the location and spread of the ground-truth return distributions. Together with the 1 1 -Wasserstein distance comparisons in Fig. 2 , these visualizations suggest that noisy return alignment helps spread the return samples while improving the accuracy of the final predictions.

sections.heading: B.2 Additional ablations on return flow hyperparameters
sections.text: In this section, we study how the two important hyperparameters in return flow affect policy performance for both VF and IVF. Because of compute constraints, we ablate these parameters on cube-triple and puzzle-4x4 with task 2 2 and task 4 4 , which are representative tasks in those domains. First, we ablate the number of flow steps used for the return flows v V v_{V} and v Q v_{Q} . Fig. 8(a) shows that different numbers of flow steps have no significant impact on policy performance for both Value Forcing algorithms. Perhaps surprisingly, 1 1 flow step can yield similar performance. Second, we ablate the number of return samples M M for estimating V V and Q Q (see Sec. 5 ). sections.heading: D.1 Dataset construction and evaluation protocol
sections.text: OGBench datasets. Following Zhou et al. (2026) , we use OGBench datasets with 100 100 M transitions ( Park et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2025a ) as the full offline dataset for cube-triple , cube-quadruple , puzzle-4x4 and humanoidmaze-giant . These datasets are collected by scripted policies: humanoidmaze-giant has trajectories with 4000 4000 time steps, and the other datasets have trajectories with 1000 1000 time steps. To subsample the full offline datasets with fractions within { 10 % , 25 % , 50 % } \{10\%,25\%,50\%\} , we draw a specific fraction of all trajectories in the offline dataset. Specifically, for each trajectory in the dataset, we compute the mean of rewards over time steps as the score and use a softmax distribution over these scores to sample trajectories without replacement. For each random seed, we sample the subset once before training and keep it fixed throughout training. OCBench datasets. We additionally evaluate 6 6 tasks from OCBench ( Park & Levine, 2026 ) : block-lite-single-task1 , block-lite-double-{task1,task2} , and chamber-lite-easy-{task1,task2,task3} . These tasks use 7 7 -dimensional actions and operate at 10 10 Hz. The lite variants have shorter horizons and simplified scripted policies compared to the original tasks ( Park & Levine, 2026 ) . We evaluate VF, IVF, and selected baselines using 25 % 25\% and 100 % 100\% of the available offline data. The full training datasets contain 10,000 10{,}000 episodes per task ( 30,000 30{,}000 for the two block-lite-double tasks), with 0.77 0.77 M transitions for block-lite-single-task1 , 5.81 5.81 M and 4.79 4.79 M transitions for block-lite-double-{task1,task2} , and 2.11 2.11 M, 3.59 3.59 M and 3.78 3.78 M transitions for chamber-lite-easy-{task1,task2,task3} . The 25 % 25\% subsets are constructed by the same procedure as for OGBench datasets. Evaluation. For evaluation, we follow a similar protocol as in Zhou et al. (2026) . For each task in the OGBench benchmarks, the agent aims to reach a fixed goal. The episode terminates if the agent reaches the goal or exceeds the maximum number of time steps: 1000 1000 for cube-triple and cube-quadruple , 500 500 for puzzle-4x4 , and 4000 4000 for humanoidmaze-giant . For OCBench tasks, the episode limits are 200 200 steps for block-lite-single , 400 400 for block-lite-double , and 500 500 for chamber-lite-easy , with early termination upon task completion. In Sec. 6.2 and Sec. 6.3 , we train all methods for 500 500 K gradient steps and, on OGBench, evaluate them every 100 100 K gradient steps for 10 10 episodes per task. On OCBench, we follow the evaluation protocol of Park & Levine (2026) and evaluate every 50 50 K gradient steps for 500 500 episodes per task, running the episodes in parallel using OCBench’s GPU-based simulator. On both benchmarks, we report the success rate at the final evaluation in Sec. 6.2 , showing the mean and one standard deviation across 4 4 random seeds. In our ablation experiments (Sec. 6.3 and Appendix B.2 ), we report the success rate averaged over the last three evaluations: 300 300 K, 400 400 K, and 500 500 K gradient steps. For figures that aggregate results over different tasks or domains, we first average the success rate at the same random seed and then compute the mean and the standard deviation over different random seeds.

sections.text: Value Flows models the return distribution using two complementary flow-matching objectives: DCFM loss and BCFM loss. The DCFM loss aims to incorporate the standard distributional Bellman equation (Eq. 1 ) into every noise level. Specifically, let v Q ​ ( z τ ∣ s , a , τ ) v_{Q}(z^{\tau}\mid s,a,\tau) denote the Q Q -velocity and p Q ​ ( z τ ∣ s , a , τ ) p_{Q}(z^{\tau}\mid s,a,\tau) denote the corresponding probability density path. sections.heading: C51 ( Bellemare et al., 2017 ) .
sections.text: C51 represents the return distribution as a categorical distribution over fixed atoms on the return support. This method minimizes the cross-entropy between this distribution and the projection of the distributional Bellman target onto the atoms. Following Dong et al. (2025) , we pair C51 with a flow BC policy and rejection sampling (Eq. 14 ).

sections.heading: IQN ( Dabney et al., 2018a ) .
sections.text: IQN is a distributional RL method that learns the full return distribution by modeling the quantile function at randomly sampled quantile fractions. This method learns to fit the quantile function using a Huber loss with a threshold κ \kappa . Following Dong et al. (2025) , we pair IQN with a flow BC policy and rejection sampling (Eq. 14 ).

sections.heading: QC ( Li et al., 2025 ) .
sections.text: Q-chunking (QC) learns a critic over action chunks with standard TD learning and selects actions by rejection sampling using a flow BC policy (Eq. 14 ).

sections.heading: VF (Ours).
sections.text: VF follows the pseudocode in Alg. 1 . We learn the Q Q -velocity and the V V -velocity using the regression objectives derived from the corresponding stochastic processes (Eq. 12 and Eq. 13 ). We learn a flow BC policy and select actions using rejection sampling as in Eq. 14 . We also use this rejection sampling to select the actions in the V V -velocity loss (Eq. 12 ). sections.heading: Implicit QC ( Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025 ) .
sections.text: Implicit QC combines the scalar Q Q and V V estimates from IQL ( Kostrikov et al., 2022 ) with best-of- N N rejection sampling from a flow BC policy. sections.heading: IVF (Ours).
sections.text: IVF follows the pseudocode in Alg. 1 . sections.heading: Hyperparameter tuning.
sections.text: Following Zhou et al. (2026) , we tune method-specific hyperparameters per domain rather than per task: we train on tasks 2 2 and 4 4 of each domain with the full dataset, and average the success rates at 500K gradient steps over tasks and seeds. sections.heading: Floq.
sections.text: We use α \alpha to denote the BC regularization coefficient. Following their original implementation, the Q Q -velocity preprocesses the noisy critic using an HL-Gauss histogram ( Imani & White, 2018 ) and preprocesses the noise level using cosine embedding. We use a uniform distribution Unif ​ ( κ ⋅ [ r min , r max ] / ( 1 − γ ) ) \textsc{Unif}(\kappa\cdot[r_{\text{min}},r_{\text{max}}]/(1-\gamma)) to sample the initial noise. We use an MLP with 512 512 units and different depths ( vel-depth ) to parameterize the Q Q -velocity. For κ \kappa and vel-depth , we reuse values from the most similar domains in the original implementations. We sweep α \alpha within α ∈ { 300 , 1000 , 3000 , 10000 } \alpha\in\{300,1000,3000,10000\} on each domain separately.

sections.heading: FlowCritic.
sections.text: To speed up training, flow rejection sampling uses M train = 4 M_{\text{train}}=4 with 1 1 Euler step (Tweedie’s formula ( Dong et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) ). During evaluation, we use M eval = 10 M_{\text{eval}}=10 with 10 10 Euler steps. For both phases, we discard the largest return sample ( m = 1 m=1 ). We do not tune hyperparameters for FlowCritic.

sections.text: Value Flows learns the return distribution with a two-member Q Q -velocity similar to the twin Q trick in Fujimoto et al. (2018) . Following the original implementation, we clip returns to the range [ r min , r max ] / ( 1 − γ ) [r_{\text{min}},r_{\text{max}}]/(1-\gamma) after every integration step of the return flow. We also clip the BC actions after every Euler step. We tune λ ∈ { 0.3 , 1 , 3 , 10 } \lambda\in\{0.3,1,3,10\} and λ w ∈ { 0.3 , 1 } \lambda_{w}\in\{0.3,1\} jointly.

sections.heading: PCBF.

We also use the same return flow clipping and action flow clipping as in Value Flows. We sweep λ ∈ { 0.3 , 0.4 , 0.6 } \lambda\in\{0.3,0.4,0.6\} on the two cube domains, λ ∈ { 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.4 } \lambda\in\{0.1,0.2,0.4\} on puzzle-4x4 , and fix λ = 0.2 \lambda=0.2 on humanoidmaze-giant .

sections.heading: C51.

sections.heading: IQN.
sections.text: IQN uses a network that takes in a quantile fraction within ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) as input, and embeds it using 64 64 -dimensional cosine features. We also use the twin Q trick from Fujimoto et al. (2018) in IQN. For estimating the Q ⁡ ( s , a ) Q(s,a) , we average the quantile predictions from 8 8 random fractions, drawn independently from a uniform distribution Unif ​ ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) \textsc{Unif}([0,1]) . sections.heading: D.4 Value Forcing improves return estimation accuracy
sections.text: For each domain, we restore a single state from the OGBench 100 100 M dataset, execute a fixed starting action chunk, and then follow a fixed data-collection policy until success or the time limit. The data-collection policy is the scripted policy with action noise or a noisy expert policy from Park et al. (2024) . From each representative state, we collect a training set and a held-out evaluation set, each with 1000 1000 trajectories. We use reward functions of cube-triple-task5 , cube-quadruple-task2 , puzzle-4x4-task4 and humanoidmaze-giant-task2 to compute the return distributions. We train VF, Value Flows, FlowCritic, PCBF, and Oracle on each training set for 100 100 K gradient steps using each method’s default hyperparameters on each domain. To evaluate the data-collection policy, all methods except Oracle bootstrap with the action chunk in the dataset (SARSA) on the training trajectories. For Oracle , it instead fits the discounted returns from different trajectories with the standard flow-matching loss (Eq. 3 ). We draw 5000 5000 return samples from each estimator at the single state and action chunk pair to visualize the predicted return histograms and compute the 1 1 -Wasserstein distance to the 1000 1000 evaluation returns. Our histograms use 200 200 bins between the 10 10 th percentile and the maximum of the ground-truth returns, widened to include all Value Flows samples. For the implicit methods in Fig. 6 , we additionally evaluate IVF, Implicit C51, Implicit IQN, and DIVL using the same training trajectories, held-out evaluation returns, and evaluation protocol described above.

sections.heading: D.5 Key design decisions in Value Forcing
sections.text: Below, we describe the alternative instantiations of RL algorithms evaluated in Fig. 5 . Since we use a target Q Q -velocity v Q ψ ¯ v^{\bar{\psi}}_{Q} to update the V V -velocity in Alg. 1 , we will use v ¯ Q \bar{v}_{Q} to simplify its notation and use p ¯ Q \bar{p}_{Q} to denote its induced noisy return distribution.

Specifically, we can remove the V V -velocity in VF and use the target Q Q -velocity at the next action a ′ ∼ π ⁡ ( a ′ ∣ s ′ ) a^{\prime}\sim\pi(a^{\prime}\mid s^{\prime}) to sample the noisy return z τ ∼ p ¯ Q ​ ( z τ ∣ s ′ , a ′ , τ ) z^{\tau}\sim\bar{p}_{Q}(z^{\tau}\mid s^{\prime},a^{\prime},\tau) . We also replace the V V -velocity v V v_{V} in the regression target with the target Q Q -velocity v ¯ Q \bar{v}_{Q} , resulting in the following objective for no value velocity : arg ​ min v Q 𝔼 s ′ ∼ p ⁡ ( s ′ ∣ s , a ) , a ′ ∼ π ⁡ ( a ′ ∣ s ′ ) τ ∼ Unif ​ ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) , ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) , z τ ∼ p ¯ Q ​ ( z τ ∣ s ′ , a ′ , τ ) [ ( v Q ( τ ( 1 − γ ) r + γ z τ + ( 1 − τ ) 1 − γ 2 ϵ | s , a , τ ) \displaystyle\argmin_{v_{Q}}\>\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s^{\prime}\sim p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a),\,a^{\prime}\sim\pi(a^{\prime}\mid s^{\prime})\\ \>\tau\sim\textsc{Unif}([0,1]),\\ \epsilon\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1),\>z^{\tau}\sim\bar{p}_{Q}(z^{\tau}\mid s^{\prime},a^{\prime},\tau)\end{subarray}}\left[\left(v_{Q}\left(\tau(1-\gamma)r+\gamma z^{\tau}+(1-\tau)\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}}\epsilon\,\middle|\,s,a,\tau\right)\right.\right. − ( ( 1 − γ ) r + γ v ¯ Q ( z τ ∣ s ′ , a ′ , τ ) − 1 − γ 2 ϵ ) ) 2 ] , \displaystyle\hskip 155.00023pt\left.\left.-\left((1-\gamma)r+\gamma\bar{v}_{Q}(z^{\tau}\mid s^{\prime},a^{\prime},\tau)-\sqrt{1-\gamma^{2}}\epsilon\right)\right)^{2}\right], where the policy π \pi is the rejection sampling policy as in Eq. 14 . This loss directly instantiates the flow Bellman backup without using the V V -velocity in the critic loss.

sections.text: Following Park et al. (2025b) , the one-step actor variant of VF replaces rejection sampling with a one-step policy π one-step ​ ( s , a 0 ) \pi_{\text{one-step}}(s,a^{0}) , where a 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I | 𝒜 | ) a^{0}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_{\lvert{\mathcal{A}}\rvert}) . Let π β ​ ( s , a 0 ) \pi_{\beta}(s,a^{0}) denote the action generated by the BC flow policy from integrating the same initial noise a 0 a^{0} . We train the BC flow policy using the standard conditional flow matching loss ℒ ⁡ ( π β ) {\mathcal{L}}(\pi_{\beta}) as in Eq. 3 . Then, the one-step policy learns to maximize the scalar Q Q estimate induced by our Q Q -velocity while distilling from the BC flow policy: arg ​ min π one-step ⁡ 𝔼 s ∼ 𝒟 , a 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I | 𝒜 | ) ​ [ − Q ⁡ ( s , π one-step ​ ( s , a 0 ) ) + α ​ ‖ π one-step ​ ( s , a 0 ) − π β ​ ( s , a 0 ) ‖ 2 2 ] , \displaystyle\argmin_{\pi_{\text{one-step}}}\>\mathbb{E}_{s\sim{\mathcal{D}},\,a^{0}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_{\lvert{\mathcal{A}}\rvert})}\left[-Q(s,\pi_{\text{one-step}}(s,a^{0}))+\alpha\left\lVert\pi_{\text{one-step}}(s,a^{0})-\pi_{\beta}(s,a^{0})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right], (28) where α ≥ 0 \alpha\geq 0 controls the strength of the distillation regularizer. Again, we compute the Q Q estimate by averaging over M M MC return samples and propagate gradients for the one-step actor through the return flow integration. For the ablation experiments, we tune α ∈ { 1 , 3 , 10 } \alpha\in\{1,3,10\} for each domain by averaging the success rates across task 2 2 and task 4 4 and choose α = 3 \alpha=3 for both cube-triple and puzzle-4x4 . In addition, we use the one-step actor π one-step \pi_{\text{one-step}} to sample actions in the V V -velocity loss (Eq. 12 ) during training and select actions during evaluation.

sections.heading: IVF with naive expectile regression.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2611.02160v1 [cs.LG] 01 Nov 2026 Value Forcing: Aligning Return Distributions at All Noise Levels Chongyi Zheng 1 Zhiyuan Zhou 2 Qiyang Li 2 Benjamin Eysenbach 1 Sergey Levine 2 1 Princeton University 2 University of California, Berkeley chongyiz@princeton.edu Abstract Learning accurate value functions is central to reinforcement learning (RL), yet remains challenging because supervision is limited and indirect: ground-truth values are unavailable, and each transition in the data only provides an immediate reward that can be used to construct bootstrapped targets as supervision. This challenge is particularly pronounced when data is limited or reward signals are sparse, as is common in real-world applications such as robotics. We argue that the key to accurate value learning in this limited data regime is extracting richer learning signals from the available data. In this paper, we introduce Value Forcing , a new approach that uses flow matching to estimate return distributions and enables accurate value learning from limited data. Our key insight is that we can extract richer learning signals by enforcing Bellman consistency at every noise level. Empirically, Value Forcing improves the accuracy of estimating the return distribution, and prevents the distribution from collapsing to a single value, as occurs with prior methods. We instantiate Value Forcing with two practical value-learning algorithms: VF, an actor-critic method, and IVF, an implicit value-learning method. We evaluate both algorithms across 26 26 long-horizon tasks in the offline RL setting and find that they outperform prior value-learning methods, with particularly large gains when data is limited. Our project website is available at https://chongyi-zheng.github.io/value-forcing . 1 Introduction Figure 1: We introduce Value Forcing , a new approach to learning distributional value functions with flow matching that supervises the learned return distribution at every flow noise level through Bellman consistency. Unlike prior methods that provide supervision only at selected noise levels or use inaccurate targets at others, Value Forcing provides substantially richer learning signals and enables much more accurate estimation of the return distribution, preventing it from collapsing around a single value. This in turn leads to better policy performance, especially in the limited-data regime. Value estimation lies at the heart of reinforcement learning (RL): value functions estimate the expected return of following a certain course of actions, guiding agents to select better actions that improve long-term returns. However, accurately estimating the values is hard, especially with limited amounts of data or if the reward feedback is sparse. Supervision for long-term value is limited and indirect: each observed transition provides only an immediate reward, but no ground-truth expected return. Temporal-difference (TD) methods construct prediction targets using their own value estimates, which could be inaccurate and bias learning. With limited data, there is little room to correct these errors. However, such settings are common in real-world applications such as robotics. This raises the question: is there a way to extract richer learning signals from limited available transitions? Many widely used RL methods ( Mnih et al., 2015 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) learn scalar value functions that summarize the future outcome of a policy. This scheme has limited expressivity and may give a sparse supervision signal when used as the target for TD learning. Distributional RL instead models the full return distribution and can provide richer learning signals when the whole return distribution is used as the TD target ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Rowland et al., 2023 ) . For example, an action that produces returns of − 1 -1 and + 1 +1 with equal probability has the same expected return as another action that always produces 0 0 return, yet their distributions differ. Learning to distinguish these two actions and their outcomes can enable more effective use of the available data. Recent work has begun to use modern generative models such as flow matching to represent the return distribution. These methods learn to map Gaussian noise to the return distribution through an iterative denoising process. Beyond capturing complex return distributions, flow matching also creates an opportunity to provide even richer supervision by learning at different noise levels ( Farebrother et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . However, prior flow-based return estimators typically only provide supervision using the endpoint of the flow path ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2025 ; Groom et al., 2026 ; Agrawalla et al., 2026 ) , missing the opportunity to supervise all other noise levels. While others have explored applying Bellman consistency at all noise levels, they either suffer from enforcing an incorrect consistency at the initial flow step ( Dong et al., 2025 ) or only apply the consistency along the flow paths starting from the same noise ( Xu et al., 2026 ) (Fig. 1 (Center) ). Empirically, we find that sparse supervision or incorrect dense supervision can lead to inaccurate modeling of the return distribution, and often results in the learned return distribution collapsing toward a point mass (see Fig. 2 ), thereby undermining the effectiveness of distributional value learning. In this paper, we introduce Value Forcing, a new distributional value learning approach that enforces Bellman consistency at every noise level (see illustration in Fig. 1 ). At each noise level, Value Forcing uses the next-state marginal return distribution to supervise the current-state marginal return distribution. Unlike the standard Bellman operator, we introduce a new flow Bellman operator that includes a Gaussian correction. We show that Value Forcing has a unique fixed point at every noise level, preserving the initial Gaussian noise and recovering the distributional Bellman equation in the denoised space. Empirically, we find that Value Forcing can model the return distribution much more accurately compared to the prior methods and does not suffer from distribution collapse (Fig. 1 ). We instantiate two practical value-learning algorithms with Value Forcing: VF, an actor-critic algorithm, and IVF, an implicit method via expectile-weighted flow matching. Theoretically, we show that IVF approaches the optimal value within actions presented in the dataset as the expectile increases. Empirically, we evaluate both VF and IVF across 26 26 long-horizon tasks, 20 20 from OGBench and 6 6 from OCBench, and show that they improve return estimation and policy performance over prior flow-based value learning methods, with particularly strong gains when data is limited. 2 Related Work Offline RL aims to learn a reward-maximizing policy from a fixed offline dataset. The core challenge in this setting is to learn a value function while preventing erroneous extrapolation outside the distribution of the dataset. Previous works have proposed strategies based on applying conservative penalties for out-of-distribution samples ( Kumar et al., 2020 ; Nakamoto et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2022 ; Chae et al., 2026 ) , constraining action selection in Bellman backups to the dataset support ( Fujimoto et al., 2019 ; Kumar et al., 2019 ; Singh et al., 2022 ) , or not querying samples outside the offline dataset at all ( Kostrikov et al., 2022 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . While most previous works focus on training an accurate value function with the entire offline dataset, we focus on the setting with extremely limited offline data. Most similar to our focus is the work of Xu et al. (2023) ; Park et al. (2026) , which also compares different value learning algorithms on subsets of the entire offline datasets. However, these methods learn a scalar return value, while we aim to learn the whole distribution of the return value using flow matching. This offers denser supervision during TD updates, and in practice leads to better performance in the limited dataset setting. We find that our method matches the state of the art on the full dataset, but outperforms it by a large margin when data is more limited. Distributional and generative value functions. Distributional value functions aim to learn the entire distribution of the discounted cumulative return instead of a single scalar that estimates its expected value ( Bellemare et al., 2017 ; Bellemare et al., 2023 ) . Early methods model the value distribution as a discrete categorical distribution ( Bellemare et al., 2017 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Dabney et al., 2018b ) or continuous distributions with restrictive modeling assumptions ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Dabney et al., 2018a ) . Recent methods have leveraged diffusion and flow matching to represent complex return distributions ( Dong et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Espinosa-Dice et al., 2025 ) and their expected values ( Agrawalla et al., 2026 ) . Our method falls into the former category, where methods differ primarily in where the Bellman consistency is enforced in the denoising path. DFC ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , FlowCritic ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) , FlowIQN ( Groom et al., 2026 ) , and Dual-Flow RL ( Li et al., 2026 ) enforce the Bellman consistency at the endpoint of the flow, where the Bellman target is computed in the denoised space and used as a flow-matching target for all noise levels. FlowIQN further introduces a quantile-aligned coupling between initial noises and final samples. Dong et al. (2025) , Espinosa-Dice et al. (2025) , and Xu et al. (2026) introduce stronger constraints along the flow path: Value Flows ( Dong et al., 2025 ) and EVOR ( Espinosa-Dice et al., 2025 ) use the velocity field directly as the TD bootstrapping target, but naïvely apply the clean Bellman equation at all noise levels; PCBF ( Xu et al., 2026 ) couples two flow paths using the same initial noise and applies the Bellman operator at all noise levels along the coupled paths, but the marginal flow paths lack Bellman consistency because of the coupling. In contrast, our method enforces the Bellman consistency at all noise levels. We achieve this by defining a flow Bellman operator whose fixed point aligns the return distributions at every noise level. We find that this results in much more accurate return estimation, especially in the low-data regime. See the Appendix Table 1 for a summary of these differences. 3 Preliminaries Markov decision process and offline RL. Concretely, we ask the research questions: (1) Does Value Forcing improve return estimation accuracy? (2) How do VF and IVF compare to prior offline RL methods across different dataset sizes? (3) What are the important design decisions in VF and IVF? Experimental setup. We evaluate our methods on 20 20 tasks from OGBench ( Park et al., 2024 ) and 6 6 tasks from OCBench ( Park & Levine, 2026 ) in the offline RL setting. OGBench includes 4 4 domains with 5 5 tasks each: cube-triple , cube-quadruple , puzzle-4x4 , and humanoidmaze-giant . OCBench includes 1 1 task from block-lite-single , 2 2 from block-lite-double , and 3 3 from chamber-lite-easy . We adopt action chunking ( Li et al., 2025 ) , where the policy predicts and executes a sequence of actions before predicting the next sequence. The resulting higher-dimensional action space makes value learning more challenging. Following Zhou et al. (2026) , we use the OGBench datasets with 100 100 M transitions as the full offline datasets and experiment with subsets of them, ranging from 10 % 10\% to 100 % 100\% , to study the effectiveness of different value learning methods on decreasing dataset sizes. For OCBench, we compare our methods with selected baselines using 25 % 25\% and 100 % 100\% of the available data. We report the mean and standard deviation across 4 4 random seeds for all experiments. See Appendix D.1 for details on dataset construction and evaluation protocols. Comparisons. We compare VF and IVF with prior value learning methods, grouped into explicit or implicit methods. For explicit methods, we compare VF against prior methods that explicitly learn a policy using flow-based distributional critics FlowCritic ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) , Value Flows ( Dong et al., 2025 ) , PCBF ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , categorical distributional critic C51 ( Bellemare et al., 2017 ) , quantile distributional critic IQN ( Dabney et al., 2018a ) , flow-based non-distributional critic Floq ( Agrawalla et al., 2026 ) , and scalar critic QC . For implicit methods , we compare IVF against prior methods that perform implicit value learning. Since there are no prior implicit flow-based distributional methods, we compare against categorical distributional critics DIVL ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , our novel adaptations of C51 and IQN termed Implicit C51 and Implicit IQN , and scalar critic Implicit QC . For OCBench experiments, we compare VF with representative baselines Value Flows, C51, and QC, and compare IVF with Implicit C51 and Implicit QC.
